entityDossier.whatItIs: The MITRE Corporation is a private not-for-profit spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1958 that operates exclusively as a manager of federally funded research and development centers. It runs six FFRDCs on behalf of the Department of Defense, the Federal Aviation Administration, Treasury and the IRS, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Health and Human Services, and NIST. It is headquartered in McLean, Virginia, and also provides the administrative home for JASON, the government's standing outside scientific advisory panel.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: MITRE is on this map because of the legal mechanism it embodies, not because a witness has named it as a custodian of material. An FFRDC is granted, by regulation, access to government and contractor data 'beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship' - including sensitive and proprietary data, installations, equipment and real property - and its sponsoring agreement gives the sponsor's Executive Agent approval authority over the classification, publication and distribution of its output. That combination produces a private organisation holding federal program records under a disclosure obligation that runs to a sponsoring agency rather than to Congress or to the public, and whose corporate files are not agency records for FOIA purposes. The DHS sponsoring agreement goes further: MITRE's own staff sign non-disclosure agreements that expressly preserve the right to report substantial violations of law to Congress, but subcontractors and consultants are required to sign the same NDA with that whistleblower carve-back removed. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison put this exact structure in writing, telling MITRE that FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records' and demanding a search back to 1 January 1930.
entityDossier.narrative:
MITRE occupies a category that exists nowhere else in the federal enterprise. It manufactures nothing, competes for nothing, and sells nothing. It exists to hold institutional memory and technical judgement on behalf of government sponsors, and the Federal Acquisition Regulation builds that role out of a single privilege: an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.' That sentence, FAR 35.017(a)(2), is the load-bearing beam of this dossier. Everything a prime contractor knows about its own black programmes, and everything the government knows about the prime, can lawfully sit inside the FFRDC that sits between them.

MITRE currently operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for DoD; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and the IRS, co-sponsored by Veterans Affairs, the Social Security Administration and Commerce; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC for NIST. Its own fact sheet notes there are only forty-two FFRDCs in total and that operating six of them is 'a high honor.' The relevant point for this board is not prestige but coverage: one nonprofit sits inside the defence establishment, the intelligence-adjacent national security enterprise, and the civil aviation regulator that owns the primary radar picture of American airspace.

The governing document that shows how this works in practice is the FY2009 sponsoring agreement between DHS and MITRE for HS SEDI, signed by MITRE's president and by the Acting Under Secretary for Science and Technology on 13 March 2009. It is worth reading as a specification for exactly the kind of custody problem this board is mapping. Section 3 states that SEDI's work 'will often require privileged access to information, including sensitive Government information and industry proprietary data not normally available to non-Government organizations.' Section 5(h) obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data.' Section 6(c)(9) records the routine practice: 'Ordinarily, sponsors release classified, privileged, no-contractor, and other sensitive material directly to SEDI.' Section 5(a) states plainly that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects.'

Then the agreement closes the loop on disclosure. Section 6(b)(9) gives the DHS Executive Agent authority to review and approve 'the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications.' Section 9(g) defines 'Privileged Information' so broadly that it captures every deliverable, note, lab record, test result and analysis MITRE produces for the sponsor, and forbids disclosure except as required by law or 'as expressly authorized in writing by the DHS Executive Agent.' Section 9(g)(2) then carves back the whistleblower statutes, stating that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.' That is the protective clause. And Section 5(j)(iv) requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2).' The people at the outer edge of the work - the ones brought in for specialised expertise MITRE does not hold in-house - are contractually bound by the secrecy terms without the clause that preserves their right to tell Congress.

This is the structural argument, and on 22 May 2026 a member of Congress made it out loud. Rep. Eric Burlison, of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, sent a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE's president Mark Peters and its general counsel Christopher Land. The relevant time period is 'January 1, 1930, to the present.' The definitions section reaches every MITRE-operated FFRDC, every subcontractor, and any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, or equivalent terms.'

The interrogatories are targeted at exactly the mechanism described above. Section III demands identification of every Special Access Program, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword and DOE SIGMA category MITRE participated in or supported in connection with UAP records, and asks whether each 'was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks MITRE to identify any classification guide, NDA, access roster or sponsor communication that instructed personnel to avoid using the terms UAP, UFO, crash retrieval or reverse engineering in records. Section VIII asks for every NDA or indoctrination instrument 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress.' Section IX asks MITRE to identify any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems or Bigelow Aerospace. Section X asks whether responsive funding was routed through a cover programme 'whose public description differed materially from the responsive work performed.' The letter warns that concealment or destruction may implicate 18 U.S.C. sections 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519 and 2071.

MITRE's reply, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was a single sentence from a spokesperson: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That answer is not evasive so much as accurate. It restates the architecture the letter was written to expose. An FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor. Congress asks MITRE; MITRE asks the sponsor; the sponsor is the same authority that classified the work. What the record does not contain, as of this writing, is the certification of search methodology, the records-location index, the preservation hold, or any production - all of which the letter demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks.

Section 9(g)(2) of the same agreement states that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law' - a protection extended to MITRE's own personnel but expressly withheld from its subcontractors and consultants.

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify any nondisclosure agreement, indoctrination record or sponsor communication 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress, Inspectors General, AARO, NARA, federal law enforcement, or appropriate cleared oversight officials.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify 'any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems, Bigelow Aerospace or its successors/affiliates.'

entityDossier.denialPosture: MITRE has not denied holding UAP-related records. Its only public statement on the Burlison inquiry, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was that it was reviewing its archives and that 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' No certification, denial of possession, or records-location index has been made public.

MITRE's role in administering JASON, and whether JASON was ever tasked on UAP or anomalous materials questions, is not addressed anywhere in the public record reviewed here.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Corporation is the largest single recipient of United States defense contract obligations, formed by the 1995 merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta. It operates cleared facilities accredited for Special Access Program work and runs the Advanced Development Programs organisation, the Skunk Works, which has built the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 among other classified aircraft. It is the only corporation named on the record, by a sworn witness in a congressional hearing, as a holder of recovered non-terrestrial material.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Lockheed Martin sits at the intersection of the two conditions this board treats as necessary for a legacy programme to survive without congressional visibility: a company with the industrial capacity to store and work on recovered material, and a legal regime that can lift normal industrial security oversight off it. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of National Industrial Security Program oversight for DoD special access programs whenever the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves a carve-out provision. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee or consultant may provide SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. Two sworn witnesses - George Knapp in September 2025 and Luis Elizondo in November 2024 - have testified to a specific, dated, blocked transaction in which material collected in the 1950s and held at a California facility was to move from a corporation to Bigelow's BAASS, and did not. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of that sworn testimony.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Lockheed Martin allegation is unusual on this board because it is the one that has been made under oath, in a hearing room, with a company name attached. On 9 September 2025, before the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, George Knapp told the committee: 'It has been widely reported and suspected that Lockheed Martin is one of the contractors - the defense contractors, that has held this stuff, stored it away in secrecy, and tried to figure out how it works.' He then went further and put his own reporting on the record: 'I have confirmed on the record that Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.' Later in the same hearing Rep. Tim Burchett asked which corporations hold the material. Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.' He added a line that is, for the purposes of this map, more revealing than the accusation itself: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Ten months earlier, on 13 November 2024, Luis Elizondo had testified to the same transaction from inside the government side of it. Asked by Rep. Burlison whether the government or defence contractors possess technology, Elizondo said one reason his predecessor programme AAWSAP was trying to collect material of unknown origin was that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material ... that was collected in the 1950s. Unfortunately, that did not actually occur.' Burlison then put the Christopher Sharp reporting to him directly - a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace, and a CIA block - and Elizondo answered: 'What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.' He described the missing instrument: 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

The official record does not name the company, but it does record the allegation. AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, logs an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.' A separate entry logs a claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly intact, under a CIA partnership that ended in 1989. AARO says it found no empirical evidence for either. AARO's denial is procedurally notable in its own right: 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, on what date, and describes no verification step beyond the meeting itself. Under this board's sourcing rule, that is an artefact of a statement, not evidence of the fact asserted.

What makes the allegation structurally survivable rather than merely unproven is the regulatory architecture around a company like Lockheed Martin. Industrial security oversight of cleared contractors is normally exercised by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency under the National Industrial Security Program. But 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.' A carve-out programme is therefore a cleared contractor facility from which the government's own standing industrial security inspector has been formally removed by name, at the direction of the second-ranking official in the Department.

The congressional side is narrowed by the same directive. DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' That is a standing prior-restraint on contractor-to-Congress disclosure inside the SAP world, in an unclassified, publicly posted directive. The statutory reporting channel is narrower still: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content of any SAP report to the defence committees on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - eight people, not four committees.

So the record on Lockheed Martin has an unusual shape. Two witnesses under oath, one of them a former Pentagon official, describing the same blocked transfer with the same missing Secretary of the Air Force memorandum. An official report that catalogues the allegation, does not name the company, and reports an unverified denial from unnamed executives. A statutory and regulatory framework that would make exactly this kind of holding invisible to the ordinary inspection and reporting machinery. And, on the other side of the ledger, no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no inventory, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record statement from Lockheed Martin responding to sworn testimony that named it.

entityDossier.whatItIs: To The Stars Academy of Arts and Science Inc. was a Delaware public benefit corporation incorporated in 2017 and registered with the SEC under Commission File Number 024-10728, CIK 1710274, EIN 82-0601064. Its directors were Tom DeLonge, former CIA Directorate of Operations officer Jim Semivan, and physicist Harold Puthoff; Lockheed Skunk Works veteran Steve Justice and former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo were listed as significant employees. It raised money through a Regulation A offering, hosted the first officially released US military UAP videos, and signed a research agreement with the US Army before winding down its aerospace work and reverting to entertainment as To The Stars Inc.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: TTSA matters to this map not as a research institution but as a legal vehicle. For roughly three years it was the corporate person through which men carrying intelligence, special-access and black-aerospace careers could act in public, hold material, sign agreements with the government, and speak to Congress and the press without a government employer's prepublication apparatus sitting on top of every sentence. Its SEC filings are the single richest primary record on this board of who those people were, what clearances and career histories they carried, and what the venture was actually organised to do. In October 2019 it converted that standing into a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering 'material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage' - a government laboratory relationship with a private company that held claimed anomalous material. AARO's own history records the same personnel network attempting to reconstitute the AAWSAP effort inside the Department of Homeland Security as the prospective special access programme KONA BLUE.
entityDossier.narrative:
To The Stars Academy is the most thoroughly documented entity on this board, for a reason that has nothing to do with UAP: it sold securities. A company that offers stock under Regulation A must file with the SEC, and the filings are public, dated, signed and auditable. The FY2017 Form 1-K is therefore the closest thing this subject has to a sworn organisational chart.

What it shows is a very small company with a very unusual staff. Officers and directors were Tom DeLonge as president and interim chief executive; Jim Semivan as vice president of operations and director; and Harold E. Puthoff as vice president of science and technology and director. The filing states that Semivan 'retired from the Central Intelligence Agency's Directorate of Operations after 25 years working as an operations officer both overseas and domestically,' that he 'was a member of the CIA's Senior Intelligence Service,' and that he 'currently holds Top Secret Clearances.' It states that Puthoff is president and chief executive of EarthTech International and director of the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin. Two significant employees are listed: Steve Justice, Director of Advanced Programs and Technology, part-time at twenty hours a week, whose industry background the filing ties to the Lockheed organisation 'known as the "Skunk Works"'; and Luis Elizondo, Chief of Security and Special Programs, full-time, described as a career intelligence officer. As of 31 December 2017 the company had eleven employees.

The financial picture in the same filing is stark. Revenues for 2017 were $1,376,215 against cost of revenues of $750,932, producing gross profit of $625,283 - essentially a merchandise and music business. The net loss for 2017 was $30,665,436, against $422,670 the prior year, almost entirely non-cash stock compensation. Gravity Holdings LLC, whose sole member is the DeLonge Family Trust, held 60,000,000 Class A shares, 85.7 per cent of the class. This was not a research budget. It was a capital structure wrapped around a founder and a small group of named individuals.

What the company did with that structure is the part that belongs on this map. It became, as the filing puts it, 'the very first company to obtain official U.S. Government footage of unidentified aerial phenomena ("UAP") that had gone through the declassification process and been approved for public release,' publishing the footage through its online Community of Interest. The videos that entered the mainstream through the New York Times in December 2017 - the material now known as FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast - reached the public through a private securities issuer, not through a Pentagon press release. That routing is itself a finding. A declassification review was completed and the product was handed to a company in which a serving-until-recently Pentagon official was chief of security and special programs.

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command 'to advance TTSA's materiel and technology innovations in order to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles.' The announcement described the technology set as leveraging 'developments in material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage,' and set out the exchange: 'TTSA will share its discoveries with Ground Vehicle System Center (GVSC) and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection (GVSP) and the U.S. Army shall provide laboratories, expertise, support, and resources to help characterize the technologies and its applications.' Dr Joseph Cannon of US Army Futures Command called the partnership 'an exciting, non-traditional source for novel materials and transformational technologies.' Steve Justice, by then TTSA's chief operating officer and aerospace division director, said the agreement brought 'additional, critically important expertise that is necessary to advance the state-of-the-art in both our near and long-term technology areas of study.'

Read against the rest of this board, the CRADA is the important document. A private company holding material it described as anomalous obtained access to Army laboratories to characterise it, under an instrument that is not a procurement contract and does not require the government to pay. A CRADA moves capability and data across the government-private boundary in both directions with far less contractual and oversight furniture than a prime contract, and it does so without a competitive solicitation. Whether or not anything anomalous was ever in those laboratories, the mechanism is precisely the kind of low-visibility government-private research channel this board is built to map.

The network did not begin with TTSA and did not end with it. AARO's Historical Record Report records that after AAWSAP was terminated, 'its supporters unsuccessfully attempted to convince DHS to support a new version of this effort dubbed KONA BLUE,' which AARO characterises as 'a UAP-related Prospective Special Access Program (PSAP) called KONA BLUE that was proposed to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and supported by individuals who believed the USG was hiding off-world technology,' and which 'was never approved by DHS.' The same people, in sequence: a DIA contract, a proposed DHS special access programme, a Delaware public benefit corporation, a congressional hearing.

Elizondo, Christopher Mellon and Justice departed in December 2020, the aerospace and materials work wound down, and the entity renamed itself To The Stars Inc. and returned to entertainment. What it leaves behind is a documentary trail that is unusually hard to argue with, because it was filed under penalty of securities law: names, ages, clearances, prior employers, share counts, losses, and an executed agreement with a US Army laboratory command.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Sol Foundation is a private non-profit co-founded by Stanford pathology professor Garry Nolan and anthropologist Peter Skafish that describes its work as science, policy and public education for what it calls the post-UAP world. It runs observational and analytical research projects, publishes a numbered white-paper and policy-briefing series, and holds an annual conference. In June 2026 five people connected to it - both co-founders, a senior adviser, an advisory board member and its production lead - were named to the US government's UAP Science Advisory Council.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Sol is the institution that converted the private technical layer into a policy actor with standing inside government. Its published output is not popular advocacy; it is a policy programme aimed squarely at the concealment mechanism, including a November 2024 paper by its own executive director on executive-branch UAP secrecy and the harm to Congress, a May 2025 paper by retired Colonel Karl Nell calling for US government disclosure, and an April 2026 briefing by its senior legislative affairs officer - a 37-year Senate Armed Services Committee staffer - proposing a whistleblower restitution fund to incentivise disclosures to Congress. Within under three years of formation, that programme placed a plurality of the members of the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject. The single largest gap in the Sol record is that it names no donors, and the board treats an unfunded map of a funding question as an open problem rather than a settled one.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Sol Foundation is the closest thing the modern disclosure effort has to a think tank, and the useful way to read it is by its bibliography rather than its press. Its publication series is numbered, dated and authored, and the sequence tells you what the organisation actually decided to work on.

The first tranche in 2024 was scoping work. Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, US Navy retired, published 'Beneath the Surface: We May Learn More about UAP by Looking in the Ocean' in March 2024, arguing that transmedium UAP and unidentified submersible objects are the overlooked domain. The foundation itself published 'UAP in Crowded Skies' in the same month and 'Anomalous Health Threats: Health Security Considerations for UAP' in July. Helen McCaw wrote on UK policy implications in May 2024. Paul Thigpen wrote on the Catholic Church's likely response in July.

Then in November 2024 Peter Skafish, the foundation's executive director and co-founder, published 'The Prospect of Executive Branch Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Secrecy: The Harm to Congress and Potential Remedies.' That is the pivot. The subject is no longer whether UAP are anomalous; it is whether an executive-branch secrecy regime has concealed decades of knowledge, research programmes and potentially retrieved technologies from Congress itself, and what remedies exist. In May 2025 the series published Colonel Karl E. Nell, retired, on 'The UFO Enigma: A Call for US Government Disclosure,' framed around the effort to revive the UAP Disclosure Act.

By 2026 the series had become numbered Science and Policy Briefings and had acquired an author who is the point of the whole exercise. Briefing No. 2, April 2026, is 'UAP Whistleblower Restitution Fund Would Incentivize Disclosures to Congress,' by Kirk McConnell. McConnell is Sol's senior legislative affairs officer and spent thirty-seven years on the staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. The paper's premise is stated at the top: individuals considering disclosing information about classified executive-branch UAP programmes to Congress face significant retaliation, including immediate loss of livelihood, and several senators have said so. That is a former SASC staffer, writing under a foundation's imprint, designing a financial instrument to overcome the deterrent that the special-access architecture places on contractor and government employees who might talk to his old committee. Briefings No. 1 and No. 3, both by Marik von Rennenkampff, cover Beatriz Villarroel's pre-satellite-era night-sky plate work and what the foundation describes as the first peer-reviewed scientific analysis of possible UAP materials, involving Garry Nolan.

That combination - a Stanford immunologist doing materials and biological analysis, a career Senate Armed Services staffer doing legislative design, an anthropologist doing the theory of secrecy - is why Sol belongs on this map. It is not a UFO group. It is a small institution that identified the mechanism, staffed against it, and published a remedy.

The consequence arrived in June 2026. Following what the foundation calls 'historic releases of government records about UAP encounters,' the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the support of the FBI, announced a UAP Science Advisory Council led by Avi Loeb, who sits on Sol's own advisory board. The foundation's announcement states that among the fourteen scientists and experts named were Sol co-founders Garry Nolan and Peter Skafish; Sol senior adviser Tim Gallaudet; and Sol advisory board member Jacob Haqq-Misra. Ross Howard, who leads production for the foundation, would lead communications for the council. The council reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board, 'an interagency body coordinating across military, law enforcement, and intelligence community agencies,' and 'All data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The foundation's own framing is unambiguous about what it thinks happened: 'The appointment of Sol's co-founders, Admiral (ret.) Gallaudet and Dr. Jacob Haqq-Misra to the government's scientific advisory body is a fulfillment of its founding mission. Sol can now share its insight to the highest levels of government deliberation about disclosure, amplifying our impact.'

Two things about that are worth holding separately. The first is a genuine institutional achievement: a private foundation went from formation to supplying a plurality of the government's outside scientific advisers on this subject in under three years. The second is a caution the board should apply without softening it: the council those people joined is, on the government's own description, unclassified-only. A body with no access to classified material cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a carve-out special access programme, and cannot compel anything. Sol's own executive director wrote the paper explaining exactly why that matters. The organisation that best articulated the executive-branch secrecy problem has now placed its people inside a body that has been constituted on the far side of the secrecy line.

The last thing to say about Sol is the thing it does not say about itself. Its site solicits membership and donations. It names no donors, no foundations and no corporate supporters. For an entity on a board whose organising question is who pays, that is the largest single documentary gap in its record, and it is not resolved by anything published as of this writing. There is also a small unresolved inconsistency in its own account of its founding date - the June 2026 announcement says the foundation 'was established in 2023,' which does not match every version the organisation has published.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The UAP Science Advisory Council is an outside scientific advisory body assembled in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the FBI and other agencies, and chaired by Harvard theoretical physicist Avi Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board that met for the first time in mid-June 2026. All data shared with the council is unclassified.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject, which makes the terms on which it was convened the most informative thing about it. Its chair has stated in writing that 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' A body with no clearances and no access to classified holdings cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a special access programme operating under a DCSA carve-out, cannot compel testimony, and cannot verify a negative. Its function, on the record as constituted, is to apply scientific method to the portion of the record that nobody disputes and that the executive branch has already chosen to release. Its membership was drawn almost entirely from the private technical and advocacy layer - the Sol Foundation and the Galileo Project - rather than from the federal laboratories, FFRDCs or prime contractors where the custody allegations point, and the published membership lists changed three times in seventeen days.
entityDossier.narrative:
The council is best understood as a boundary object: an institution created at the seam between a declassification programme and a scientific community, whose terms of reference tell you exactly where the executive branch has decided that seam sits.

The origin story is not disputed by anyone involved. The Skeptics Society announcement of 15 June 2026 says the council was 'formed at the request of the White House and in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and other agencies.' Avi Loeb's own account, published on Medium and dated by the platform to 13 June 2026, says: 'Over the past week, I was tasked by the above organizations to create a research team of young scientists who will serve on this council,' naming the White House, AARO, ODNI, the FBI and all Intelligence Community members. The Sol Foundation's account says ODNI, with the support of the FBI, announced it. DefenseScoop obtained confirmation from an ODNI official that ODNI, alongside the FBI and DoD, established the UAP Governance Board 'to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies,' and that the board 'met for the first time yesterday' as of Wednesday 17 June 2026, without identifying the participants.

The membership is where the record becomes genuinely strange, and the board should record the instability rather than smoothing it into a single roster. Loeb's first post named a core research team of five: Richard Cloete, Regina Sarmiento, Matthew Szydagis, Devesh Nandal and Omer Eldadi. The Skeptics Society, two days later, published an alphabetised list of eleven, adding Tim Gallaudet, Garry Nolan, Michael Shermer, Peter Skafish and Jennice Vilhauer, and identifying Loeb as chair. The Sol Foundation described a fourteen-member council and additionally named Jacob Haqq-Misra and Ross Howard. Loeb's list supplied to DefenseScoop on 17 June named twelve and introduced Carol Cleland and Ben Lamm while dropping Sarmiento. His second Medium post, dated by the platform to 29 June, listed fifteen and added Liberty Vittert Capito, Robin Hanson and Kevin Knuth while restoring none of the dropped names. Four published lists in seventeen days, none of them identical, none of them issued by the government that convened the body. There is no charter, no Federal Advisory Committee Act notice, and no agency-published membership roster in the record reviewed here.

The operative constraint is stated by the chair himself, twice, in plain language: 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The Sol Foundation repeats it. DefenseScoop reports that Loeb 'confirmed that all of the data shared with the newly installed team will be unclassified.' Loeb also told DefenseScoop that the meeting cadence has not been decided, and closed with a formulation that is worth quoting exactly because it is candid about the position: 'We will make the best lemonade out of the lemons we are given.'

Set that against what the council would need in order to test the central allegation on this board. The custody claims concern material held at contractor facilities under special access protection. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), the Director of DCSA can be relieved of industrial security oversight of exactly such a facility by a Deputy Secretary of Defense-approved carve-out. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee may hand SAP material to a member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. A council with no clearances is on the outside of both of those doors. It cannot look at a carve-out programme, cannot subpoena a contractor, cannot inspect material, and cannot verify that the archival material it is given is complete. Its chair says the council's purpose is to advise on how to resolve the nature of UAP and, in support of the Governance Board, to 'assist in the timely coordination of declassification of UAP-related information, in accordance with Executive Order 13526.' That is a real function. It is also, structurally, an advisory role over the release of material that the classification authorities have already decided to release.

The second structural observation is about where the people came from. Loeb chairs the Galileo Project at Harvard; Cloete and Sarmiento are described in the Skeptics Society announcement as Galileo Project researchers. Nolan and Skafish co-founded the Sol Foundation; Gallaudet is a Sol senior adviser; Haqq-Misra sits on Sol's advisory board; Ross Howard leads Sol's production and was named to lead the council's communications. Nobody named to the council in any published list is identified as coming from a federal weapons laboratory, an FFRDC, a University Affiliated Research Center, or a prime contractor's advanced development organisation. The council is staffed from the community that has been asking the questions, not from the institutions that would hold the answers.

None of that is a criticism of the individuals, several of whom have argued publicly for exactly the kind of instrumentation and data quality that would move this subject forward. It is a statement about the shape of the instrument. The government convened an outside body, gave it distinguished members and a reporting line to an interagency board, and drew the boundary of its access at the classification line - the same line on the far side of which every substantive allegation this board catalogues is alleged to sit.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program was a Defense Intelligence Agency effort solicited publicly on 18 August 2008 as HHM402-08-R-0211 by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity and awarded on 22 September 2008 as firm-fixed-price contract HHM402-08-C-0072 to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, LLC of Las Vegas. Its stated objective was to understand the physics and engineering of breakthrough aerospace weapon system applications out to the year 2050 across twelve technical areas. It ran to 2012 and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents plus a much larger body of work that has never been released.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: AAWSAP is the only documented instance in the modern record of the United States government funding a private company to study the physics of observed anomalous flight performance, and its own procurement file shows the seams through which such work escapes normal visibility. The solicitation was posted as a total small business set-aside under a classification code meaning 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' place of performance was the contractor's own facility, and the Top Secret facility clearance requirement was formally amended so that it was not required prior to contract implementation. The statement of work provides that any accountable property the contractor acquires with government funds becomes government-owned property and must be inventoried and returned within sixty days of contract end - a custody provision whose closeout has never been publicly documented. Senator Harry Reid asked the Deputy Secretary of Defense to convert the effort into a special access program on 24 June 2009 and was refused. The unreleased output of this contract, which its own government manager has described as running to more than a hundred detailed reports, is the largest identified block of missing documentary material in the modern record.
entityDossier.narrative:
AAWSAP is the best-documented UAP effort in the history of the United States government, and the reason is mundane: it was a competed commercial-items procurement, so it left a paper trail that the Freedom of Information Act could reach.

The solicitation went up on FedBizOpps as a combined synopsis/solicitation on 18 August 2008 under number HHM402-08-R-0211, issued by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity at Bolling AFB, with responses due 5 September 2008. It was coded B, 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' under NAICS 541330, Engineering Services, and it was 'solicited as a total small business set aside' with a size standard of twenty-five million dollars. The Statement of Objectives, dated 18 July 2008, is unambiguous about what was wanted: 'The objective of this program is to understand the physics and engineering of these applications as they apply to the foreign threat out to the far term, i.e., from now through the year 2050. Primary focus is on breakthrough technologies and applications that create discontinuities in currently evolving technology trends. The focus is not on extrapolations of current aerospace technology.' Twelve technical areas were named, covering lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament including directed energy, and other peripheral areas.

The qualification language is the tell. Offerors were asked to 'provide examples, conducted within the past 7 years, of having performed, as a prime contractor, the analysis, design, construction, and flight testing of high performance aircraft and/or satellites,' with the note that 'Success in this program is dependent upon this capability and experience.' The government was not shopping for a literature review.

The award document, Standard Form 1449, records contract HHM402-08-C-0072, awarded 22 September 2008 to BIGELOW AEROSPACE ADVANCED SPACE STUDIES, LLC, 4640 S Eastern Ave, Las Vegas NV, CAGE 54JU7, DUNS 827037768, with a total award amount of $21,948,810.00 and a base year of 22 September 2008 to 29 September 2009 followed by option years. The solicitation had anticipated 'a base year of 12 months from date of award plus four (4) 12 month option years' running to 30 September 2013. Deliverable line items were status reports, a project management plan for tasks 3.a.1 through 3.a.12, research reports for the same tasks, a Comprehensive Integrated Threat Assessment, travel and other direct costs.

Three provisions in the statement of work matter more than the money. First, security: 'The contractor shall comply with the terms and conditions of the DD-254 BEFORE initiating any classified effort,' and 'Contractor shall provide a work facility (including unclassified information systems) with a Top Secret Facility Clearance granted by the Defense Security Service (DSS).' But an amendment posted with the solicitation changed DD Form 254 Block 13 from 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE GRANTED BY THE DEFENSE SECURITY SERVICE (DSS) PRIOR CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION' to 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL NOT BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE ... PRIOR TO CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION. HOWEVER, IT MUST BE OBTAINED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE DURING THE INITIAL YEAR OF THE CONTRACT.' The facility-clearance bar was lowered before award.

Second, place of performance: 'The work under this contract shall be performed at the Contractor's facility.' Third, and most consequential for this board, property: 'Any accountable property acquired by the contractor with government funds during the execution of this contract shall become government owned property. ... This property must be inventoried and returned to the government not more than 60 days after the end of the contract.' There is, in the released file, no closeout inventory.

What the contractor actually did is not seriously in dispute, and AARO concedes it. AARO's Historical Record Report states: 'Although investigating UFO/UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organization conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager. This research included: reviewing new cases and much older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.' AARO adds that 'DIA did not seek, nor specifically authorize, this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract with the private sector organization,' and that the effort also investigated an alleged hotspot of UAP and paranormal activity at a Utah property then owned by the head of the contractor.

The special access question is the hinge. AARO records that 'On 24 June 2009, Senator Reid sent a letter to then Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Deputy Secretary Lynn declined to do so based on the recommendation of then-Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, James R. Clapper, Jr., that such a designation was not justified.' That refusal is documented in the FOIA record alongside DIA talking papers prepared for Reid's visits to the Director of DIA in January and May 2009 and an eighteen-page packet presented to the Deputy Secretary in November 2009.

AARO's account and the contractor's account of what the programme produced differ by an order of magnitude. AARO says the contract 'produced exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed,' and that it 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work.' The releasable record contains thirty-seven of thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. What is not in the record is the 494-page BAASS Ten Month Report, the Utah ranch investigation report, the personnel roster, obligation-by-year funding data, and the balance of the material that the government programme manager has described as running past a hundred reports. Under this board's sourcing rule, AARO's characterisation is a Tier 2 record of what AARO said, not a Tier 1 record of what exists.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Defense Intelligence Reference Documents are a series of approximately thirty-eight unclassified technical survey papers commissioned from outside specialists under the AAWSAP contract and published by the Defense Intelligence Agency between roughly 2009 and 2011. They cover metamaterials, warp drive, traversable wormholes, antigravity, negative mass propulsion, quantum vacuum energy extraction, invisibility cloaking, high-frequency gravitational wave communications, and human biological effects of anomalous fields. Thirty-seven of the thirty-eight were released to The Black Vault by DIA on 25 March 2022 under FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The DIRDs are the most literal artefact on this board: a list, written by the United States government's own defence intelligence agency, of every theoretical route by which the observed flight performance of anomalous objects might be achieved. Read as a set, they are not a scattershot survey but a systematic decomposition of a capability - lift without visible propulsion, translation in space and time, signature reduction, materials that do not behave conventionally, and the effects such a craft would have on a human body standing near it. The government commissioned this taxonomy in 2008 and 2009 while the same contract was running field investigation teams and proposing laboratories to examine recovered material. One of the thirty-eight, the classified SECRET version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons,' has never been released and was not even acknowledged as withheld in the release letter, which is why the requester appealed on the adequacy of the search rather than on an exemption.
entityDossier.narrative:
There is a way of reading the DIRD series that makes it the single most informative document set on this board, and it is simply to read the titles in order and ask what question they collectively answer.

The released thirty-seven include 'Metallic Glasses - Status and Prospects for Aerospace Applications,' 'Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter,' 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms,' 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications' and 'Metallic Spintronics' - the materials question. They include 'Positron Aerospace Propulsion,' 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion,' 'Advanced Nuclear Propulsion For Manned Deep Space Missions,' 'Negative Mass Propulsion,' 'Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion,' 'Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion II,' 'MHD Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications' and 'Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites' - the propulsion question. They include 'Warp Drive, Dark Energy, and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions,' 'Advanced Space Propulsion Based on Vacuum (Spacetime Metric) Engineering,' 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy,' 'The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research,' 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications,' 'Concepts for Extracting Energy From the Quantum Vacuum' and 'Quantum Tomography of Negative Energy States in the Vacuum' - the physics-you-would-need question. They include 'Invisibility Cloaking - Theory and Experiments' and 'Detection and High Resolution Tracking of Vehicles at Hypersonic Velocities' - signature and detection. And they include 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues,' 'Biosensors and BioMEMS,' 'Biomaterials,' 'Technological Approaches to Controlling External Devices,' 'Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft' and 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' - the human question, which is to say, what happens to a person near one of these, and what would it be like to be inside one.

That is not a random reading list. It maps one to one onto the twelve technical areas in the AAWSAP statement of objectives: lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament, and peripheral areas. The DIRDs are the deliverable structure of the contract made visible. And two of the titles are difficult to explain by any framing other than the one this board starts from. 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues' is a medical paper about injury from proximity to something. 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' is a human factors paper about operating a vehicle that does not exist.

The release history is its own artefact. Eric Davis, who worked for Bigelow Aerospace and BAASS, said on Coast to Coast AM on 28 January 2018 that thirty-eight such reports had been produced under AAWSAP. Within forty-eight hours The Black Vault filed for all of them; the request became FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018. In January 2019 a listing breakdown of the reports arrived under a separate case, FOIA-0033-2019, though a slightly different version of the list had already leaked. DIA completed the main request more than four years later, on 25 March 2022, releasing thirty-seven of the thirty-eight. The one that did not come out was the SECRET-classified version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons.' Critically, it was not listed as withheld. The release letter did not reference it at all, which is why the appeal was filed on the adequacy of DIA's search rather than on the applicability of an exemption - a procedurally different and, for a board about concealment, a more interesting posture. An unclassified version of that same paper, DIRD 23, is in the released set at thirty-one pages.

The DIRDs also function as a personnel map. The authorship of the series connects the private technical layer catalogued elsewhere on this board directly to a DIA contract: the space-time metric engineering and quantum vacuum papers, the wormhole and warp drive papers, and the materials papers were written by named specialists who reappear later at To The Stars Academy, at EarthTech International, and in the disclosure hearings of 2023 to 2025. The government did not go to a federal laboratory or an FFRDC for this survey. It went to a small network of physicists with an existing interest in the subject, through a small business set-aside contract, performed at the contractor's own facility.

What the series does not contain is equally important and should be stated plainly. No DIRD reports an examination of recovered material. No DIRD describes a craft. They are literature surveys and theoretical assessments, and several of them conclude that the routes they examine are not presently achievable. AARO's characterisation is that they were 'exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed.' On the face of the documents, that is accurate.

The argument for their place on this map is therefore not that they contain the secret. It is that they define its shape. A government office that believed it was looking at nothing would not commission a paper on the acute and subacute effects of anomalous fields on human biological tissue. A programme whose only interest was foreign aerospace threat out to 2050 would not need a survey of traversable wormholes. The DIRDs are the negative space around an object: thirty-eight independent attempts to explain, from first principles, how something that had already been observed could possibly work.

claims.text: The Defense Intelligence Agency released thirty-seven of the thirty-eight AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Documents to The Black Vault on 25 March 2022, completing FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018, which had been filed on 31 January 2018.

The one report not released was the SECRET-classified version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons'; it was not referenced as withheld in the release documentation, so the administrative appeal was filed on the adequacy of DIA's search rather than on an exemption.

The released series includes 'Warp Drive, Dark Energy, and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions' (DIRD 13, 33 pages), 'Advanced Space Propulsion Based on Vacuum (Spacetime Metric) Engineering' (DIRD 15, 17 pages) and 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy' (DIRD 18, 42 pages).

The released series includes 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications' (DIRD 19, 44 pages), 'The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research' (DIRD 14, 16 pages) and 'Negative Mass Propulsion' (DIRD 29, 43 pages).

The released series includes 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues' (DIRD 26, 38 pages), a survey of physiological effects on humans from proximity to anomalous fields.
The released series includes 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' (DIRD 28, 57 pages), a human-factors assessment of operating a vehicle with capabilities beyond current aerospace technology.

The released series includes 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications' (DIRD 22), 'Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter' (DIRD 02), 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms' (DIRD 05), 'Metallic Glasses - Status and Prospects for Aerospace Applications' (DIRD 01) and 'Invisibility Cloaking - Theory and Experiments' (DIRD 07).

The subject coverage of the series maps onto the twelve technical areas specified in the AAWSAP Statement of Objectives of 18 July 2008: lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial/temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament, and peripheral areas.

Eric Davis stated in a Coast to Coast AM interview on 28 January 2018 that while working for Bigelow Aerospace/BAASS he and colleagues created thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents under AAWSAP, which is what triggered the FOIA request that eventually produced the release.
A separate FOIA case, FOIA-0033-2019, produced a listing breakdown of the reports in January 2019, a slightly different version of which had already leaked before official release.

AARO characterises the DIRDs as 'exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' and states that 'These scientific papers were never thoroughly peer reviewed.'

AARO states that the DIRDs represent essentially the whole of what AAWSAP produced, that it 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work conducted by AAWSAP/AATIP,' and that the remainder of the effort consisted of case reviews, interviews of observers, and work on alleged paranormal activity at the contractor principal's Utah property.

No released DIRD reports the examination of recovered material or describes a recovered craft; the released series consists of literature surveys and theoretical assessments, several of which conclude the routes examined are not presently achievable.
The tasking record showing who inside DIA selected the thirty-eight DIRD topics, and on what basis each was chosen, has not been released.

entityDossier.denialPosture: DIA has not denied the existence of the series; it released thirty-seven of thirty-eight papers under FOIA in March 2022. Its release documentation made no reference to the classified SECRET version of the high-energy laser weapons report, neither producing it nor logging it as withheld. AARO's position is that the papers are unreviewed exploratory surveys tasked under the contract's stated aerospace-threat scope.
openQuestions: The status of the thirty-eighth document, the SECRET version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons,' and the outcome of the adequacy-of-search appeal.
The internal DIA tasking record: who chose the thirty-eight topics, when, and against what requirement. No topic-selection memorandum has been released.

Whether any of the DIRD authors held or were offered special-access read-ins in connection with the work, which would connect the unclassified series to a classified effort.
